Dass Bewerberinnen oft schlechter bewertet werden als männliche Mitbewerber, ist nichts Neues. Doch inzwischen treffen nicht mehr nur Personalverantwortliche diese Entscheidung, sondern algorithmische Systeme. So sperrte etwa ein Lieferdienst einem Schwarzen Fahrer den Zugang zu seinem Arbeitsaccount, weil die biometrische Identitätsprüfung ihn nicht erkannt hat – denn marginalisierte Gruppen sind in Datensätzen unterrepräsentiert, sodass die Gesichtserkennungssoftware höhere Fehlerraten aufweist. Auch im Gesundheitskontext treffen algorithmische Systeme folgenreiche Entscheidungen. So werden Herzinfarkte bei Frauen unter anderem deswegen häufiger nicht erkannt, weil es in der medizinischen Forschung an Daten zu Frauen fehlt (sog. Gender Data Gap), sodass Diagnosesysteme vornehmlich mit männlichen Symptomen trainiert und weibliche Symptome damit von den Diagnosesystemen häufiger übersehen werden. Solche Fälle beruhen auf sog. algorithmischer Diskriminierung – doch diese wird im aktuellen Reformentwurf des Allgemeinen Gleichbehandlungsgesetzes (AGG) nicht berücksichtigt.
Algorithmische Diskriminierung als Leerstelle im AGG

Seit Juni 2026 berät der Bundestag über die Änderung des AGG. Ziel ist es, in Deutschland die Rechte von Personen zu stärken, die von Diskriminierungen betroffen sind (so die Bundesregierung). Insofern erstaunt es, dass der aktuelle Gesetzentwurf eine wesentliche Entwicklung übergeht, die nach zwanzig Jahren AGG auf der Hand liegt: die KI-Transformation. Diese Lücke kritisierte im Oktober 2026 auch der Sachverständige Alexander Tischbirek. Er führte aus, dass das Szenario diskriminierender KI illustriere, „wie sich die einzelnen Defizite des Entwurfs im konkreten Fall wechselseitig verstärken“ könnten.

Dass Entscheidungen, die algorithmengesteuerte Systeme – insbesondere KI1) – treffen, diskriminieren können, ist inzwischen vielfach empirisch belegt. Algorithmische Diskriminierung ist darauf zurückzuführen, dass die Systeme – anders als es den Anschein hat – keine neutralen Werkzeuge sind. Sie lernen vielmehr aus Daten, die bestehende gesellschaftliche Ungleichheiten widerspiegeln. Zudem werden sie überwiegend in einem Umfeld entwickelt, in dem Frauen und andere marginalisierte Gruppen deutlich unterrepräsentiert sind. Dies erhöht das Risiko, dass Diskriminierungspotenziale übersehen werden. Algorithmische Systeme reproduzieren diese Ungleichheiten nicht nur, sondern skalieren sie auch: So treffen sie in zahlreichen (grundrechtssensiblen) Anwendungsbereichen diskriminierende Entscheidungen, etwa beim Recruiting, bei der Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung, in der Medizin oder im öffentlichen Sektor, insbesondere im Justizvollzug. Algorithmische Systeme benachteiligen Beschäftigte zudem bei der Zuteilung von Arbeit und der Bewertung ihrer Leistung (sog. algorithmisches Management), Verbraucher:innen bei der Bepreisung von Produkten und geben Nutzer:innen vor, was sie in sozialen Netzwerken sehen (wie z.B. Jobanzeigen).

Die Nichtberücksichtigung von algorithmischer Diskriminierung im Rahmen der AGG-Reform ist auch deshalb bemerkenswert, weil es sich um ein dem Bundestag wohlbekanntes Phänomen handelt: So kündigten CDU/CSU und SPD bereits im Koalitionsvertrag der 19. Legislaturperiode an, algorithmenbasierte Entscheidungen für Verbraucher:innen überprüfbar zu machen (S. 135), und wiederholten dies (sinngemäß) im aktuellen Koalitionsvertrag (S. 69). Daneben hat das Bundesministerium für Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend algorithmische Diskriminierung an zahlreichen Stellen in seinem Dritten Gleichstellungsbericht aufgegriffen, und auch die Antidiskriminierungsstelle benennt die fehlenden Regelungen ausdrücklich und umfassend als Defizit.
Die verfassungsrechtlichen Vorgaben

Diese Leerstelle tangiert die Gleichheitssätze aus Art. 3 Abs. 2 und 3 GG. Diese Grundrechte verpflichten den Staat in zweierlei Hinsicht: Zum einen darf der Staat nicht selbst diskriminierende KI einsetzen oder solche unkritisch übernehmen (Abwehrfunktion der Grundrechte). Zum anderen ist er auch in der Pflicht, einen Regelungsrahmen zu schaffen, der solche Benachteiligungen erkennbar und angreifbar macht und insbesondere eine effektive Rechtsdurchsetzung gewährleistet (Schutzfunktion der Grundrechte, vgl. Sachs/Nußberger/Hey, 10. Aufl. 2024, GG Art. 3 Rn. 65 ff., 233 ff.). Grundrechtsträger:innen haben somit ein Recht darauf, dass der Staat sie auch gegenüber Grundrechtsbeeinträchtigungen durch Private – in Form von ungerechtfertigten Benachteiligungen – schützt. Diesen Schutz soll das AGG verwirklichen. Doch wenn der Gesetzgeber bei der AGG-Reform gerade durch neue Technologien typische Benachteiligungen außer Acht lässt, wird er seiner Schutzpflicht nicht gerecht.
Algorithmische Diskriminierung

Um das Phänomen algorithmischer Diskriminierung dem AGG zuordnen zu können, muss man es zunächst verstehen. Kurz gesagt entsteht algorithmische Diskriminierung durch das Zusammenwirken technischer und gesellschaftlicher Ursachen. Maßgeblich ist insbesondere, dass die algorithmischen und KI-Systeme auf Trainingsdaten beruhen, die entweder historische Ungleichheiten abbilden oder nicht repräsentativ sind und damit z.B. die Gender Data Gap beinhalten. Lernen Algorithmen auf dieser (fehlerhaften) Datengrundlage, so verfestigen sie die gelernten Muster und vervielfachen sie in Form von Outputs (sog. Garbage-in-Garbage-out-Prinzip). Gewichtet ein Recruiting-System etwa Bewertungskriterien wie „Teilzeit“ negativ, weil es die potenziell „arbeitsbereitesten“ Mitarbeitenden auswählen soll, erscheint dies zunächst plausibel. Zugleich werden damit jedoch strukturelle Ungleichheiten fortgeschrieben, da oftmals Personen in Teilzeit arbeiten, die Care- und Pflegearbeit leisten oder in Alleinerziehenden-Konstellationen leben (vgl. Legner, RDi 2024, 426, 429). Zudem bleibt oft unentdeckt, dass Datensätze in der Aufbereitung verzerrt werden und die Systeme während des Trainings diskriminierend entscheiden. Das hat mit dem sog. Black-Box-Charakter von KI-Systemen zu tun: Viele KI-Systeme beruhen auf sog. Deep-Learning-Methoden und neuronalen Netzen (siehe u.a. Martini, Blackbox Algorithmus, S. 23, Plaue, Data Science, 19-2 (2021)). Damit lässt sich kaum nachvollziehen, wie die KI die Wahrscheinlichkeiten berechnet, die uns Menschen als Output – in Form von Entscheidungen – trifft, z.B. „sollte zum Auswahlgespräch eingeladen werden“ bzw. „sollte nicht zum Auswahlgespräch eingeladen werden“ (s. Hoffmann-Riem, AöR 2017, 1 (29)). Verstärkt werden die Ursachen durch die weitgehend homogene Tech-Branche, die Benachteiligungen für marginalisierte Gruppen schlicht übersieht (sog. Privilege Hazard, D’Ignazio/Klein, Data Feminism).
Die Logik des AGG

Das AGG verhindert Benachteiligungen wegen der Rasse oder der ethnischen Herkunft, des Geschlechts, der Religion oder Weltanschauung, einer Behinderung, des Alters oder der sexuellen Identität (§ 1 AGG). Unmittelbare algorithmische Diskriminierung liegt vor, wenn eine Person wegen eines geschützten Merkmals eine weniger günstige Behandlung erfährt (§ 3 Abs. 1 AGG). Dies ist z.B. der Fall, wenn das Merkmal „Geschlecht“ unmittelbar als Entscheidungsvariable dient und das System systematisch Bewerbungen von Frauen ablehnt. Mittelbare algorithmische Diskriminierung liegt vor, wenn scheinbar neutrale Faktoren (sog. Proxys) verwendet werden, aus denen das System Rückschlüsse auf geschützte Merkmale zieht (vgl. § 3 Abs. 2 AGG) – etwa wenn es erlernt, dass die „Elternzeit“ statistisch mit dem Geschlecht zusammenhängt und eine Kreditvergabe deshalb ablehnt. Allerdings verschwimmen die Grenzen zwischen unmittelbarer und mittelbarer Diskriminierung, da die diskriminierende Ursache aufgrund der Datenmenge und der Intransparenz des Entscheidungsvorgangs oft nicht nachvollziehbar ist (vgl. Spiecker gen. Döhrmann/Towfigh, Automatisch benachteiligt, 2023, S. 19 f.).

Lücken bestehen in doppelter Hinsicht: Einerseits erfasst das AGG intersektionale Diskriminierung, also Benachteiligungen, die erst aus dem Zusammenwirken mehrerer geschützter Merkmale entstehen, nur unzureichend. § 4 AGG regelt Mehrfachbenachteiligungen lediglich für die Rechtfertigung. Gerade algorithmische Systeme benachteiligen aber häufig an solchen Schnittstellen, wie das Beispiel kommerzieller Gesichtserkennungssysteme bei Schwarzen Frauen zeigt: Diese werden deutlich schlechter als weiße Männer erkannt. Andererseits erfassen die in § 1 AGG aufgeführten Merkmale gerade keine Benachteiligungen, die sich aus einer Kombination vermeintlich neutraler Kategorien ergeben, aber keinem geschützten Merkmal eindeutig zuzuordnen sind. Soll ein algorithmisches System z.B. über die Kreditwürdigkeit von Personen entscheiden, bildet es Gruppen („kreditwürdig“, „nicht kreditwürdig“), die nicht (nur) auf dem „Geschlecht“ oder der „ethnischen Herkunft“ beruhen, sondern auf Faktoren wie etwa dem Endgerät, dem E-Mail-Anbieter oder etwaigen Angaben im Lebenslauf. Wenn sich diese auf „algorithmischen Gruppen“ beruhende Vorauswahl keinem geschützten Merkmal eindeutig zuordnen lässt, fallen etwaige Benachteiligungen aus dem Anwendungsbereich des AGG.
Massenhaft schutzlos

Verschärfend kommt hinzu, dass das AGG zivilrechtliche Schuldverhältnisse nicht hinreichend erfasst. Das Gesetz schützt zwar bei Verträgen zwischen Privaten vor Diskriminierung (sog. zivilrechtliches Benachteiligungsverbot, § 19 AGG). Für die Merkmale Geschlecht, Religion, Behinderung, Alter und sexuelle Identität gilt dieses Verbot jedoch – neben privatrechtlichen Versicherungen (§ 19 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 AGG) – nur bei sog. Massengeschäften und massengeschäftsähnlichen Geschäften (§ 19 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 AGG). Allein Benachteiligungen aus Gründen der Rasse oder wegen der ethnischen Herkunft (sowie in Zukunft ggf. des Geschlechts, vgl. § 19 Abs. 2 AGG-E) sind darüber hinaus auch in allen zivilrechtlichen Schuldverhältnissen verboten (§ 19 Abs. 2 AGG). Massengeschäfte sind solche, die typischerweise „ohne Ansehen der Person“ zustande kommen (MüKoBGB/Thüsing, 10. Aufl. 2025, AGG § 19 Rn. 17); bei massengeschäftsähnlichen Geschäften kommt dem Ansehen der Person nachrangige Bedeutung zu (BGH NJW 2020, 852 Rn. 20 f.). Die algorithmischen Systeme zeichnen sich jedoch gerade dadurch aus, dass sie eine Vielzahl von Einzelfallentscheidungen treffen (Spiecker gen. Döhrmann/Towfigh, Automatisch benachteiligt, 2023, S. 76). Den Verwender:innen geht es um die automatisierte Optimierung der eigenen Bedingungen. Mit anderen Worten betreiben algorithmische Systeme massenhafte Individualisierung (vgl. Spiecker gen. Döhrmann/Towfigh, Automatisch benachteiligt, 2023, S. 28): Gerade weil algorithmische Systeme massenhaft benachteiligen, dabei aber jede Entscheidung auf die einzelne Person zuschneiden, droht ihnen das Merkmal „ohne Ansehen der Person“ zu fehlen, an das § 19 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 AGG den Diskriminierungsschutz knüpft. Geschäfte, in denen algorithmische Entscheidungen den Alltag prägen – Kreditvergabe, Scoring, personalisierte Preissetzung – drohen deshalb, aus den zivilrechtlichen Benachteiligungsverboten i.S.d. § 19 Abs. 1 AGG herauszufallen.

items.titel: Schwarz-Rot verschiebt Zuckersteuer
items.anriss: Im Ringen um den Haushalt hat sich die Koalition nach ARD -Informationen auf einen Kompromiss geeinigt. So soll etwa die Einführung einer Zuckersteuer verschoben werden - zudem wird die Stromsteuer wohl vorerst nicht für alle gesenkt.[ …

absaetze.t: Haushaltsberatungen Zuckersteuer verschoben - keine Einigung bei Stromsteuer

Im Ringen um den Haushalt hat sich die Koalition nach ARD-Informationen auf einen Kompromiss geeinigt. So soll etwa die Einführung einer Zuckersteuer verschoben werden - zudem wird die Stromsteuer wohl vorerst nicht für alle gesenkt.

Die schwarz-rote Koalition hat sich in ihren Haushaltsberatungen nach Informationen des ARD-Hauptstadtstudios in mehreren Streitpunkten auf Kompromisse verständigt. Die Zuckersteuer auf stark gesüßte Getränke soll nun erst Anfang 2028 kommen und damit einige Monate später als geplant. Eine geplante neue Steuer auf Plastikverpackungen soll im nächsten Jahr vorerst nicht erhoben werden. Die von Kanzler Friedrich Merz stark unterstützte Senkung der Stromsteuer für alle wird zugleich immer unwahrscheinlicher.

Die Fraktionen von SPD und Union kamen am Abend zu Sondersitzungen zum Haushalt zusammen. Während die SPD nach einer Dreiviertelstunde fertig war, ziehen sich bei der Union die Gespräche. Die Koalition steht mit ihren Verhandlungen unter Zeitdruck, da an diesem Donnerstag der Haushaltsausschuss des Bundestags zur sogenannten Bereinigungssitzung zum Etat 2027 zusammenkommen soll.
Zuckersteuer in drei statt zwei Stufen

Die Zuckersteuer sollte nach dem ursprünglich vom Kabinett auf den Weg gebrachten Entwurf zum 1. Juli 2027 starten. Die Union hatte sich aber für einen späteren Start zum 1. Januar 2028 eingesetzt, auch um Herstellern etwa von Limonaden die Umstellung von Rezepturen zu ermöglichen. Erhoben werden soll die Steuer ab Anfang 2028 nunmehr in drei statt zwei Stufen nach dem Zuckergehalt.

Union und SPD hatten die Einführung der Steuer im Zuge des beschlossenen Gesetzes für stabile Krankenkassenbeiträge verabredet. Gelten soll sie etwa für Colas, Limonaden, Eistees, Energydrinks und Fruchtsaftgetränke mit Zuckerzusatz.
5,4 Milliarden für Stromsteuersenkung gesucht

Bei der geplanten Stromsteuersenkung fanden Union und SPD bisher keine Finanzierung. Theoretisch könnten die Fraktionen die nötigen rund 5,4 Milliarden Euro morgen bei der Haushaltsbereinigungssitzung zwar noch gegenfinanzieren, der Haushalt ist aber bereits extrem eng. Bisher haben die Haushälter keine Spielräume gefunden. Damit ist unwahrscheinlich, dass die Entlastung zu Jahresbeginn - wie von Merz gewünscht - kommen kann.

Union und SPD hatten im Koalitionsvertrag festgelegt, die Stromsteuer für alle auf das europäische Mindestmaß zu senken. Umgesetzt wurde dies aber bisher nur für das produzierende Gewerbe und die Land- und Forstwirtschaft.
Kein Ausgleich der Kalten Progression

Die Union wollte zudem erreichen, auch die inflationsbedingte Kalte Progression vollständig auszugleichen. Dazu konnten die Fraktionen nach Informationen des ARD-Hauptstadtstudios keine Einigung erzielen. Insbesondere in der Unionsfraktion soll das die Stimmung gedämpft haben.

Eine Verständigung erzielt wurde dazu, geplante Kürzungen bei sozialpolitischen Vorhaben zurückzunehmen. Weniger Einsparungen als ursprünglich geplant wird es etwa beim Elterngeld, Wohngeld und Unterhaltsvorschuss geben.
Die Alkoholsteuer soll wie geplant ab Januar angehoben werden, die Schaumweinsteuer soll hingegen nicht steigen.

items.titel: France's 11 November ceremonies: Macron, Le Pen, Mélenchon between memory and pacifism
items.anriss: Marking the 108th anniversary of the 1918 armistice, Emmanuel Macron led the ceremony at the Arc de Triomphe, while Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon chose symbolic venues to deliver their messages months before the presidential …

absaetze.t: France commemorated this Wednesday the end of the fighting of the First World War. As every year, the 11 November ceremonies brought together elected officials, members of the armed forces, veterans and citizens around war memorials across the country. But this year's events inevitably had a political dimension, with several contenders in the presidential election taking part, each choosing their own location and message.
ADVERTISEMENT

In Paris, Emmanuel Macron presided over the national ceremony under the Arc de Triomphe. It was his last 11 November as head of state. The president first paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau, laying a wreath in front of his statue on the Champs-Élysées, before heading to Place de l'Étoile. After reviewing the troops, he rekindled the flame of the Unknown Soldier and observed a minute's silence.

The names of five service members who have died for France since the start of the year were then read out. Among them were adjudant-chef Thibaud Breteau, who died in the Levant, major Arnaud Frion, killed in Iraq, as well as three soldiers who died in Lebanon: adjudant Florian Montorio, sergent Anicet Girardin and caporal-chef Florian Gillet.
La Marseillaise was then sung by the army choir.

The head of state did not speak during the ceremony. However, he posted on X, stating that "Le Bleuet de France is the memory of those who have died for France. It expresses our solidarity with those who still bear the scars of History," and adding that "behind every uniform, there is courage. Behind every sacrifice, a family. Behind every hero, France that remembers."
In Hénin-Beaumont, Marine Le Pen calls for national unity

It was in her stronghold of Pas-de-Calais that Marine Le Pen chose to commemorate 11 November. The RN presidential candidate paid tribute to soldiers killed in action, but also to the women who remained on the home front during the conflict.

In her speech, she stressed the need to preserve collective memory and keep alive the sense of national belonging. "Honouring their memory, we commit ourselves to preserving the values for which they fought: sovereignty, freedom and love for our homeland."

Evoking the spirit of resistance and sense of duty of the Poilus, the name given to French soldiers during WW1, Marine Le Pen called for collective action in the face of hardship: "Faced with the misfortunes of the country, we cannot remain spectators or commentators," insisting that national cohesion cannot be built on a loss of bearings or on amnesia.
In Creuse, Jean-Luc Mélenchon chooses a pacifist monument

For his part, Jean-Luc Mélenchon opted for a less conventional trip. The La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) leader travelled to Gentioux-Pigerolles, in the Creuse department, centre of France, to take part in the ceremony in front of the village war memorial. This is a highly symbolic site, known for its inscription "Cursed be war". The monument depicts an orphan raising his fist towards the names of soldiers killed in combat, as shown in a photo in this post on the presidential candidate's X account.
A tribute marked by pacifism and anti-militarism, which makes Gentioux-Pigerolles a rallying point for activists committed to these ideas.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon's choice is therefore no accident. The France Unbowed candidate, who had already visited the site in the past, framed his speech around remembrance and a rejection of war.

"I come here because, like many others, I believe that whoever does not know their history and has not reflected on it is exposed to seeing it repeat itself, without being able to recognise its features when it comes. It is our mission, we Unbowed, to carry History," he said.

He also hammered home his opposition to any preparation for conflict: "Down with war! We will not wage it, we will not organise it, we will not prepare it!", a pacifist message that echoes his recent statements on Ukraine.

At a rally last Saturday in Le Bourget, Jean-Luc Mélenchon defended the idea of "consulting" the inhabitants of Donbas, largely occupied by the Russian army, about their future, as part of a settlement of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

This proposal earned him a firm response from Ukrainian diplomacy, which recalled that Ukrainians, including the inhabitants of Donbas, had already chosen their borders at the 1991 independence referendum.

This Wednesday in Gentioux-Pigerolles, the France Unbowed leader also called for national unity, which he considers inseparable from that of the French people, while denouncing racism and hatred of others.

items.titel: Hormuz Strait will ‘never return’ to pre-war status, Iran’s Ghalibaf says
items.anriss: Iran's parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions.

absaetze.t: Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions for ending war.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran.

In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict.

“There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he said.
Seven conditions
Ghalibaf said Tehran provided a clear response to the US through a Qatari mediator that included its seven conditions for peace talks, adding that Iran is waiting for an official response.
“The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Iran’s conditions, as outlined by the chief negotiator, include lifting the US-imposed naval blockade and sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
He said these demands were part of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and their implementation was necessary before entering negotiations with the US.
“If America limits itself to what has been agreed upon without making excessive demands or engaging in behaviour that breeds distrust, then, naturally, reaching an agreement is possible,” he said.
“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States.”
Renewed conflict
Ghalibaf said US officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to mediate direct negotiations with Tehran during a visit to Moscow.
He warned against new US attacks against Iran, saying that US President Donald Trump will face another defeat and political pressure from the new Congress that takes office in January.
Iran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, he said, urging a sustainable deterrent capability, including military capabilities.
Yemen mediation

On the ongoing fighting in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for “Supporters of God”), Ghalibaf said that “no one should interfere” in it.
“If both the government in Yemen and Saudi Arabia were to ask for our help, we would certainly offer our assistance to help resolve their conflict,” he said.
Iran has previously offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group in October following a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

items.titel: German ministries spend €5.8 million on office décor, drawing taxpayers' criticism
items.anriss: Citizens face burdens and service cuts, while the federal government spends millions on furniture, lamps and decor, claims the Taxpayers' Association.

absaetze.t: Published on 11 November 2026 - 21:58 GMT+1

Since the start of the current legislative term in May 2025, the federal government has spent around 5.8 million euros on new furniture, furnishings and decorations. This emerges from a government response to a parliamentary question from the AfD group in the Bundestag.
ADVERTISEMENT
The figures have now triggered sharp criticism from the German Taxpayers' Association.
Its president, Reiner Holznagel, is particularly critical of what he sees as a contradiction between calls for savings directed at the public and the spending within the machinery of government.

"There is supposedly no room to relieve the burden on citizens, but when it comes to their own government apparatus, the belt is pretty loose - for decor and the like!", Holznagel told the German newspaper Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung.
Foreign Office, Defence and Finance most spending

Spending by the 16 federal ministries has totalled about 5.8 million euros since May 2025. The figures cover not only classic items of furniture but also lamps, carpets, curtains, paintings, sculptures and ornamental plants.

The Foreign Office was particularly free with its money. There, spending on furniture, lamps, carpets and decoration has added up to €840,062 since the start of the legislative term. In 2026 alone, around €256,000 went on lamps, carpets and curtains.

In second place comes the Defence Ministry with around €813,000. The Federal Finance Ministry has also recorded substantial expenditure. Since May 2025, the department led by Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) has invested more than half a million euros in furniture, equipment and decoration.
Finance Ministry tops the league

Particularly striking is a look at decoration costs alone. Here, the Finance Ministry heads the list. Since May 2025, it has spent a total of €45,077 on decorations. That means more than a quarter of the federal government's total decoration spending is accounted for by this ministry.
The Finance Ministry has also incurred substantial costs for office furnishings at the senior management level. In 2026 alone, 47,737 euros have so far been spent on refitting the relevant offices.
Taxpayers' association calls for more responsible spending policy

For the German Taxpayers' Association, the figures are a reason to question the federal government's spending policy in principle. Holznagel argues that anyone demanding thrift from citizens must apply the same standards within their own authorities and ministries.
He sees the Bundestag's budget committee as having a particular responsibility. It can now demonstrate how seriously politicians take the savings measures they have announced.

The debate is likely to raise the broader question of how responsibly the federal government handles taxpayers' money. Especially at a time of strained public finances, the public is likely to watch closely how politicians spend their money.

items.titel: Ukraine Regretting White House-Brokered Temporary Ceasefire In Strategic Riverside Town Of Oleshky
items.anriss: Ukrainian officials are expressing major regrets about a White House-brokered temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, which sits on the Russian-held side of the Dnipro River, the body of water that serves as a dividing line between the opposing …

absaetze.t: Ukrainian officials are expressing major regrets about a White House-brokered temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, which sits on the Russian-held side of the Dnipro River, the body of water that serves as a dividing line between the opposing forces. Kyiv is concerned Russian forces will once again use this decimated locale to bombard Kherson City with cross-river drone and artillery attacks.

As many as 2,000 Ukrainian citizens were left in this town at the edge of the front line, caught between drone and artillery volleys launched by both sides. Intensive Ukrainian drone operations had largely ran the Russians out of Oleshky and a wide swath of territory as far as 30 km behind the lines, according to the Kyiv Post, citing Russian sources. This had reduced, but not prevented, Russian attacks against the Ukrainian side of the river. As we reported last year, Moscow’s forces have been carrying out widespread drone strikes on largely civilian targets in this region for quite some time in order to wear down the population, primarily in the large city of Kherson just across the river.

The military governor of the Kherson region has claimed that Russia took advantage of the ceasefire, brokered by First Lady Melania Trump to restore its forces in the bombed-out town. The statements by Oleksandr Prokudin follow comments made by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and a Ukrainian military officer that the Russians moved troops and equipment into the area under the cover of the ceasefire and will use them to step up attacks across the Dnipro.

“It took us about a year to eliminate what they have now restored during the ceasefire,” Prokudin told Ukrainian Pravda. “They have restored almost everything. They used this time very effectively: they carried out personnel rotations, rebuilt completely destroyed positions, and resupplied themselves with food, generators, and fuel.”
During the ceasefire, the Russians moved drones, artillery and ammunition into Oleshky, Prokudin stated.
“Furthermore, enemy troops searched Oleshky for basements to set up new hideouts for drone operators,” the Ukrainian official noted, adding that an increase in enemy strikes should be expected.

“Currently, the occupiers are launching approximately 700–800 drone attacks per day, deliberately terrorizing the civilian population of Kherson and the coastal communities,” he said. “They will 100% increase.”
A video of Russian forces moving back into Oleshky, which you can see below, emerged on social media on Nov. 2, the day after the ceasefire ended.
Russia has not officially commented on these claims, which TWZ cannot independently verify. We reached out to Melania Trump’s office for comment about the Ukrainian claims.
How Did The Ceasefire Come To Be?

Home to some 24,000 people before the all-out Russian invasion, Oleshky was captured as the Russians pushed toward the Dnipro River. With the city now largely in ruins after more than four years of conflict, the population, as we noted earlier in this story, had dwindled to fewer than 2,000, mostly senior citizens and children unable to get out, according to the White House. In October, First Lady Melania Trump brokered a deal that would allow many of those residents to leave.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” the First Lady said in announcing that the localized ceasefire, the first of its kind, would commence Oct. 29. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”

The First Lady and her representative “worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire,” the statement added. “The First Lady initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary.”

After several rounds of negotiations, the ceasefire ultimately began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time on Oct. 27 and ended late on Nov. 1, said Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who called it the longest such arrangement since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Lubinets and David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky’s parliamentary faction, were the Ukrainian negotiators. After the ceasefire ended, both men praised the operation and Melania Trump held a press conference at the White House to announce the results.
How The Ceasefire Worked
The operation unfolded in several stages, Lubinets said, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).

“After the cease-fire took effect, Russian forces began demining roads leading to Oleshky, a process that continued through Oct. 29,” the publication stated. “Humanitarian supplies, including food, medicine, drinking water, and specialized hospital equipment, were then delivered.”

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, accompanied by their teams and journalists from Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia, “subsequently entered the occupied city to oversee the distribution of aid and assist residents seeking evacuation,” the outlet added. “Residents were given three options: remain in Oleshky and receive humanitarian assistance, leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory, or travel to Russia or territory under Russian control.”

During this effort, the Ukrainian delegation “experimented with drone surveillance and direct communication between Ukrainian and Russian military representatives to monitor compliance,” the news outlet noted. “Arakhamia said the experience had helped demonstrate how localized cease-fires could be verified rather than relying solely on competing military intelligence claims.”

“All people who wanted to be evacuated from Oleshky to Ukraine are now in Ukraine,” Lubinets said, adding that he had “personally overseen the evacuation process and spoken with residents to establish whether their decisions were voluntary.”
Lantratova concurred that the ceasefire went off as planned in terms of the humanitarian goals.
“I can state that there were no incidents or violations of the ceasefire,” she said, according to Russian media. “Everything went exactly as planned.”
Ukraine Soon Expressed Regret
As noted earlier in this story, Ukrainian officials began to express concerns about the military results of the ceasefire about a week after it ended.
Russia brought more than 1,000 troops into the area under the cover of the ceasefire, an officer with the unit defending the Ukrainian side of the Dnipro claimed on Nov. 6.

“Russian forces have massed in positions from which they had been driven out over the past six months, effectively moving about 20 kilometers closer to the line of contact,” Yaroslav Moroz, head of the Unmanned Systems Department of the 34th Separate Marine Brigade of the Ukrainian Navy, told RFE/RL. “Prior to the ceasefire, the situation on the left bank of the Kherson region was different: the Armed Forces of Ukraine had expanded their engagement zone, pushed the enemy back, and severed their logistics.”

“There are no massive assault operations at the moment. However, we are prepared for them,” Moroz added. “Russian forces have brought a large quantity of equipment and ammunition into the Oleshky hospital, knowing that the Armed Forces of Ukraine would not attack the building, as local residents are receiving medical treatment there.”
Two days later, Zelensky complained about the Russian advances in the region.

“Unfortunately, under the cover of a humanitarian operation in Oleshky, the Russian army carried out a major rotation of personnel and equipment on the left bank,” the Ukrainian leader stated on X. “Additional occupation forces were brought into Oleshky and the surrounding community. The command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine must present proposals for additional protection of lives in Kherson from Russian terror.”

Ukrainian officials took the calculated risk that making a deal with Russia would benefit a large number of people caught in the middle of a brutal conflict. After what Ukrainians claimed transpired following the ceasefire, the future of such endeavors is unclear.

items.titel: Plans To Fly Talon Blue CCA Drone From British Carrier Confirmed By Northrop Grumman
items.anriss: The Royal Navy is aiming to see Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) drone fly from a British aircraft carrier next year. The planned demonstration is another notable step toward a carrier-based CCA capability …

absaetze.t: The Royal Navy is aiming to see Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) drone fly from a British aircraft carrier next year. The planned demonstration is another notable step toward a carrier-based CCA capability in the United Kingdom. The plans also signal significant new opportunities on the horizon for Talon Blue, the first flight of which was only announced last month.

“We look forward to working with the Royal Navy over the next 12 months on this future demonstration,” Northrop Grumman told TWZ in a statement today. “Thursday’s signing is an important step in demonstrating relevant British naval capabilities, building on Northrop Grumman’s decades of leadership in autonomy and commitment to mission-relevant platforms and systems.”

First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins had first announced plans to launch Talon Blue, which the U.S. military has also designated the YFQ-48A, from a carrier during an address yesterday at the International Sea Power Conference in Norway. Jenkins, the first Royal Marine to ever hold the post of First Sea Lord, the United Kingdom’s top naval officer, made his remarks aboard the HMS Prince of Wales. That ship is the second of two Queen Elizabeth class carriers in Royal Navy service today.

“In two days’ time, on this carrier, I will sign a statement of intent with our friends at Northrop Grumman to prepare their Talon demonstrator for trials with the Royal Navy under Project Vanquish,” Jenkins declared to those in attendance. “Through that agreement, we will work towards a demonstration in U.K. waters in 2027, including a launch from the carrier.”

The planned tests involving Talon “will give us the evidence we need to understand how uncrewed combat aircraft can operate safely and effectively alongside the existing air wing. Then we learn, adapt and keep moving forward,” he continued. “That is how we deliver capability at the pace necessary. Not by waiting years for a perfect solution, but by working with industry to get the latest technology into the hands of our people as quickly as possible. Of course, moving at pace carries some risk.”

Jenkins first announced Project Vanquish in September 2025. As outlined then, the project’s goal was to demonstrate the ability to launch and recover what authorities in the U.K. refer to as a Tier 2 Autonomous Collaborative Platform (ACP) from a carrier without the need for a catapult or arresting gear. The Royal Navy’s Queen Elizabeth class carriers are so-called short-takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) types that lack catapults and arresting gear, but there has been talk in the past about adding those features in some form down the line.

In the British government’s parlance, Tier 2 ACPs are defined primarily by being ‘attritable.’ This, in turn, is generally taken to mean designs that are low-cost enough to be employed in higher-risk environments from which they may not return, but that are also capable enough to conduct relevant missions.

Since Talon Blue was first officially disclosed in December 2025, at a media event that TWZ attended, Northrop Grumman has talked about the design as being lower-cost. However, the company does not appear to have used attritable or similar terms to describe the drone. Hard cost data of any kind has yet to be disclosed. Talon Blue does appear to be in line, broadly speaking, with the complexity of the two CCAs now in production for the U.S. Air Force. Those drones, General Atomics FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril’s FQ-44A Fury, are understood to have unit costs in the low tens of millions

“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness,” Craig Woolston, Vice President and General Manager for Research and Advanced Design, at Northrop Grumman said in a statement accompanying the announcement of Talon Blue’s maiden flight last month. “We listened. Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities. Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”

What it might take to configure Talon Blue for carrier-based operations remains to be seen, even without the need for the drone to be capable of catapult launches and arrested recoveries. An entirely new variant could well be required, if it is not already in the works.

It should be noted that the Royal Navy has already demonstrated the ability to launch and recover several different types of propeller-driven drones from the decks of its Queen Elizabeth class carriers since 2023. This includes the Mojave from General Atomics in the United States. Just earlier this month, the service announced that the Tekever AR5 had joined this list. The British Army is already in the process of acquiring AR5s for land-based use to replace its long-troubled Watchkeeper drones. None of these drones are as advanced as the jet-powered Talon Blue.
The Royal Navy has also launched other smaller drones, including long-range one-way-attack types, from its Queen Elizabeth class carriers via trailer-mounted catapults in the past.

All of this has been in sevice of a broader Royal Navy push to incorporate more uncrewed platforms with higher degrees of autonomy into its operations in the air and at sea. The service has dubbed this broader vision as its Hybrid Navy concept.

“I do not believe the Royal Navy can build the Hybrid Navy at the speed we need it by doing things the way we have always done,” First Sea Lord Jenkins said yesterday, speaking about these plans more broadly. “During my career, I have seen too many examples of what happens when institutions become too set in their ways. So I need industry alongside us from the start.”

The decision to involve Northrop Grumman Talon Blue also represents a significant development for that drone. The company has said the genesis behind this uncrewed aircraft was lessons learned from its failed bid in the first phase, or Increment 1, of the U.S. Air Force’s CCA program. Especially since it received its U.S. military designation, Talon Blue has looked well positioned for the Air Force’s follow-on Increment 2 CCA competition.

Northrop Grumman is also one of the companies under contract now to develop a conceptual carrier-based CCA design for the U.S. Navy. The company has yet to share details about what that proposed drone might look like, but a demonstration of Talon Blue operating from a British carrier could provide hints.

The market space for land- and carrier-based CCAs has also expanded globally. Talon Blue is just one of several notable new designs to break cover in this arena in recent years, including in the United Kingdom. This development trend also extends to potential adversaries, and China in particular.

The CCA market could be differently important for Northrop Grumman going forward given the company’s recent loss to Boeing in the U.S. Navy’s F/A-XX next-generation carrier-based fighter competition. Back in 2023, Northrop Grumman had also dropped out of the running for the U.S. Air Force competition that led to the F-47, which is also being built by Boeing. Northrop Grumman is the prime contractor for a number of other very high-profile U.S. military programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and the LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM).

Plans to launch Talon Blue from a British carrier are still very much in their infancy, but the demonstration now on the horizon for next year looks set to be an important development for all parties involved.

In a new low for an art world we thought had reached rock bottom, Artnet has announced an official partnership with the betting platform Kalshi in an incestuous marriage of two markets known for financial opacity, insider trading, and the most insufferable straight men you've ever met: art and predictions.

The news came in a press release ahead of New York's marquee auction week, promising interested budding criminals users an exclusive opportunity to “trade yes-or-no contracts in a peer-to-peer structure” (??) on public art sales. The mechanism is as follows: Artnet will use its Price Database, once nostalgically the realm of wannabe art advisors trying to sound like they have an MBA, to “curate" (help) “events” (HELP) such as whether a lot will exceed its estimate. Surprising no one, Miami Art Week in December will be the “next major moment” for the partnership, bro.

absaetze.t: The best part of the new documentary about the famed artist is watching people interact with his work.
November 11, 2026 — 2 min read

A new documentary about Romare Bearden embraces a collage-like sensibility, fitting well with the artist’s most influential work. Romare Bearden: A Life in Collage, soon to screen at DOC NYC, eschews the familiar structure of a linear biography, jumping around to find thematic rhymes through different periods of Bearden’s life.
Early on, for instance, the film alludes to Bearden’s family’s participation in the Great Migration, but rather than dwell on his biography, it turns to the recurring motif of trains in his work.

The film benefits from generous access to recordings of Bearden himself, who speaks with remarkable elegance about his memories, artistic process, and influences. Shaped by living in the South, Harlem, and Pittsburgh, his studies at the Sorbonne, and his time in the military and semiprofessional baseball during the first half of the 20th century, Bearden synthesized them into an oeuvre now seen as emblematic of the broader Black experience of the era.

items.titel: As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate
items.anriss: Efforts are underway to restore vernacular architecture and historic signage along the route of America’s most famous highway, which opened 100 years ago this month

absaetze.t: US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.
Linking diverse cultures

“We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” says Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”

Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.

“You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”

Advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.

“It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is important and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”

Local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a new Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.

The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.

Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, says that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”

Most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the new visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.

“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm says.

Projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.

items.titel: Ozette, la « Pompéi » amérindienne, et ses 50 000 objets figés dans la boue : l’art des Premières Nations du Nord-Ouest américain à l’honneur au musée du quai Branly
items.anriss: C’est une étroite bande de terre, s’étirant de l’Alaska au nord de l’Oregon, où prospère un environnement d’une grande diversité. Rivières poissonneuses fourmillant de saumons, profonds fjords, forêts denses d’épicéas, faune variée …

absaetze.t: C’est une étroite bande de terre, s’étirant de l’Alaska au nord de l’Oregon, où prospère un environnement d’une grande diversité. Rivières poissonneuses fourmillant de saumons, profonds fjords, forêts denses d’épicéas, faune variée comprenant autant de mammifères marins que d’ours, cervidés, des multitudes d’oiseaux… Dans ce cadre fertile et cette luxuriance sont nées des sociétés de pêcheurs-chasseurs-cueilleurs, des sociétés fortement stratifiées – composées de captifs, de gens du commun et de personnages de haut rang –, dirigées par un chef dont l’autorité et le prestige dépassaient largement les frontières du village ou du clan. Un univers à découvrir à partir du 29 septembre.
20 000 av. J.-C: premières traces archéologiques

On estime qu’environ 200 000 personnes vivaient dans ces régions avant l’arrivée des Européens, et qu’on y parlait au moins quarante-cinq langues appartenant à treize groupes linguistiques différents. Encore lacunaire, l’archéologie révèle que le peuplement de la côte s’est fait, comme pour le reste de l’Amérique, via la traversée du détroit de Béring par des groupes originaires d’Asie, autour de 20 000 avant notre ère. Avec le recul des glaciers, les populations migrèrent peu à peu vers les îles et le littoral, et se rassemblèrent en petites communautés structurées vers 5500-2500 av. J.-C. Les familles installées près des cours d’eau les plus peuplés de saumons devinrent alors parmi les plus aisés et finirent par acquérir le statut d’élites. L’humidité du climat ne favorisant pas la conservation des artefacts en bois, ce sont surtout des objets en pierre et en os qui attestent du degré de sophistication de ces premières sociétés.

Coiffe frontale dite « chapeau de clan », motif d’ours et plongeon à gorge rouge, culture Tlingit, Alaska, Etats-Unis, v. 1860, bois sculpté et peint, haliotide, peau et tendons, 30 x 17,5 x 23 cm, Paris, musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac. © Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac/Patrick Gries.

Mais la découverte la plus importante fut, dans les années 1970, celle du village d’Ozette, sur le littoral de l’État de Washington, véritable « Pompéi du Nord-Ouest », qui allait révéler un pan entier de l’histoire de cette région. Un glissement de terrain ayant sans doute provoqué une coulée de boue figea pour l’éternité quatre maisons en bois et plus de cinquante mille objets, offrant aux archéologues un tableau saisissant du mode de vie de leurs habitants. Vers l’an 1500, des artistes réalisaient ainsi des massues en os de baleine, des bols et des boîtes sculptés dans le bois, ainsi que des vanneries d’une finesse arachnéenne. Il existait, bien avant le contact avec les Européens, une grammaire stylistique extrêmement codifiée allant du figuratif à l’abstraction, qui allait envahir aux siècles suivants tous les pans de la création.
Hameçon, Colombie-Britannique, Canada, s.d., bois, os et ficelle, 17 x 12,5 x 1,5 cm, Paris, musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac. © Muséedu quai Branly – Jacques Chirac.

Grand Corbeau, « le plus intelligent des oiseaux » S’il est une figure récurrente chez les peuples autochtones de la côte nord-ouest, c’est bien le corbeau. Affecté des mêmes qualités et défauts que les humains, il est celui qui, dans la mythologie haïda, s’empare avec ruse du soleil enfermé dans une boîte. C’est lui également qui libère des créatures d’une palourde géante et donne ainsi naissance aux Haïdas. Facétieux et destructeur tout à la fois, il peut se prendre à ses propres pièges, mourir et réapparaître. Reconnaissable à son long bec et à ses yeux dilatés, sa silhouette se déploie sur tous les supports – masques, mâts héraldiques… –, et jusqu’au monde contemporain, dans cette sculpture de Bill Reid intitulée The Raven Discovering Mankindin a Clamshell (1970).

Bill Reid, The Raven Discovering Makind in a Clamshell, culture haïda, Colombie-Britannique, Canada, 1970, buis sculpté, 7,6 x 7 x 6,2 cm, Vancouver, Museum of Anthropology, University of British Columbia. © Museum of Anthropology at UBC, Vancouver, Canada.
Symboles, mythes et identité claniques : une koinè culturelle

Avant les ravages de la colonisation et son cortège de drames (déshérence des cultes, épidémies, interdiction du potlatch…), ces populations – Tlingits et Tsimshians vivant sur les côtes de l’Alaska, Haïdas installés sur les îles aujourd’hui appelées Haida Gwaii, autrefois de la Reine-Charlotte, Salish répartis entre les rivages de la Colombie-Britannique et l’intérieur des terres – habitaient ainsi dans de larges maisons communautaires et partageaient tout un patrimoine de rites et de croyances, ainsi qu’un système de représentations exceptionnel dans le monde amérindien.

Hochet-corbeau, culture haïda, Colombie-Britannique, Canada, avant 1882, bois sculpté et peint, 31,5 x 11 x 11 cm, Paris, musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac. © Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac/Claude Germain.

Composés de créatures surnaturelles et d’une multitude de signes confinant à l’abstrait, leurs innombrables objets d’art revêtaient ainsi une signification tant religieuse que sociale, affirmant la puissance d’une famille ou d’un clan, le caractère ancestral d’un lignage hautement vénéré. Des mâts héraldiques dressés devant les façades des maisons jusqu’au décor des vêtements, des cuillers, des bols ou des coffres, on décèle le même foisonnement de formes hybrides dans lesquelles l’œil exercé devine ici un bec, là les yeux démesurément agrandis d’un oiseau. « C’est un art de la propagande, une forme de communication visuelle redoutablement efficace qui continue d’être partagée de nos jours par l’ensemble des groupes culturels de la région, avec des variantes locales », résume Steve Bourget, un des commissaires de l’exposition.
Bol, s.d., bois d’aulne, 12 x 20 x 11 cm, Londres, The British Museum. © GrandPalaisRMN (The British Museum)/The Trustees of the British Museum.
